content.overview: A sensor can be accurate at its location and still be unrepresentative of the crop. Specialist verification separates placement effects, local microclimate and instrument bias before a reading drives a control decision.

vocabulary.definition: How well a measurement reflects the process or crop condition relevant to the decision.
Placing instruments together under the same exposure to distinguish location differences from instrument disagreement.
A measurement difference caused by location, shielding or exposure rather than the process condition of interest.

sections.title: Location can create real differences
sections.body: Wall, return-air, equipment-discharge and canopy sensors may legitimately differ because they measure different microclimates. Verify the measurement question before declaring an instrument wrong.

sections.title: Colocation separates instrument from location
sections.body: When sensors disagree, colocated comparison under the same exposure helps reveal whether the difference follows the devices or the locations.

sections.title: Use independent evidence before major changes
sections.body: Compare neighboring sensors, verified references, crop response and equipment state before letting one outlier drive a high-consequence control action.

workedExamples: A canopy sensor reads warmer after being moved closer to a fixture; placement/radiant-load bias should be checked before labeling it inaccurate.
commonMistakes: Assuming installed controllers are automatically the most accurate source.
content.practicalApplication: Classify five sensor locations as representative, local-purpose or suspect for a supplied room map and justify each decision.
content.summary: Sensor quality begins with the question the sensor is supposed to answer.
